entities.name: Armenian National Assembly
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The National Assembly of Armenia (Azgayin Zhoghov), the unicameral parliament of the Republic of Armenia established after independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, is the central legislative institution of one of the South Caucasus's most politically dynamic states — having experienced two revolutions (1998 and 2018), intermittent electoral fraud controversies, and the aftermath of the devastating 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war that resulted in Armenia's effective loss of the disputed territory.

The National Assembly was established under Armenia's 1995 constitution and initially operated under presidential-parliamentary hybrid governance. The 2015 constitutional amendments (passed 63% to 32% in a controversial referendum) transformed Armenia from a presidential to a parliamentary system, making the Prime Minister the dominant executive and reducing the President to a ceremonial role. This transition shaped the context of Nikol Pashinyan's 2018 Velvet Revolution — when massive peaceful street protests forced Prime Minister Serj Sargsyan to resign just days after assuming the role despite promising not to — and Pashinyan became PM.

The 2020 Armenia-Azerbaijan war over Nagorno-Karabakh — in which Azerbaijan rapidly recaptured most of the territory with Turkish-supplied drones, ending with a Russian-brokered ceasefire — created profound political crisis in Armenia, with opposition demanding Pashinyan's resignation for military failure. The 2021 elections returned Pashinyan with a majority, and the National Assembly has subsequently managed the aftermath of the Karabakh defeat, Azerbaijan's September 2023 offensive that resulted in the flight of 100,000+ ethnic Armenians from Karabakh, and delicate diplomacy with Azerbaijan, Russia, EU, and the US.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Armenia's National Assembly — arena of the 2018 Velvet Revolution, parliamentary manager of the catastrophic 2020 Karabakh defeat, and institution navigating Armenia's existential geopolitical repositioning between Russia and the West — is the central democratic institution in one of the most crisis-tested small states in the post-Soviet world.
